A team adds SSR to an app that has run in browsers for years. The first server render fails with
in the theme service, so they wrap that line in

from the analytics service, and each one gets its own check. A week later there are dozens of checks, one of them sits in a template and causes a hydration mismatch on every article page, and the next library upgrade breaks the server again, this time at import, where no check can reach.
The belief: component code is browser code. SSR is an extra step that happens somewhere else, so when a line fails on the server, you fence that one line off with

It's a reasonable starting point. For most of an Angular app's life, every line did run in a browser. The error names one global on one line, and wrapping that line makes the error disappear, which feels like a fix. Answers online often show exactly that pattern. What's missing is a picture of what the server actually executes, and without it you guard lines one crash at a time instead of designing for two platforms.
The server runs your whole app
To produce HTML, the server bootstraps the same application in a server runtime such as Node.js. Routes are matched, services created, components constructed, inputs set,
called and templates evaluated, just as in the browser. The SSR guide lists what isn't there: browser-specific globals like
at build time runs the same code too, so a static page has the same constraints as a server-rendered one.

That's why one check per crash never converges. Any code reachable from bootstrap can run on the server: a field initializer, a service constructor, a guard, a pipe. And module-level code runs when the file is imported, before any component exists, so a library that touches
at import time fails before your check could ever run.
Render hooks are the browser-only lifecycle
Angular already has a place for browser-only work. The lifecycle guide says render callbacks "do not run during server-side rendering or during build-time pre-rendering", and the SSR guide recommends
for code that relies on browser-specific symbols.
runs once after the next render, which suits a third-party widget or a scroll listener;
runs after every render, for measurements that must stay current. Both must be called in an injection context, typically the constructor.

content.text: The right version has no platform check at all. The server renders the bar at 0%, the browser renders the same markup, and only after that render does the callback attach the listener. The cleanup sits next to the setup, so the listener can't outlive the component.

Not every difference is about timing. Reading a saved theme is a real question on both platforms with different answers. Here the SSR guide is explicit: prefer platform-specific providers over runtime checks with
. Components inject one abstraction, and each platform registers its own implementation.

isn't banned. A single check inside one service, for a decision that doesn't change what's rendered, is fine. The problem is using it as the default tool: every check is a branch where the two platforms do different work, and the checks spread to wherever the last crash happened instead of living in one place.
